body: The two have exactly the same four letters, and even the function order does not change with the suffix. The difference appears only in the Identity layer inside a 16Personalities report: one end is more at ease with its own judgement, the other more readily doubts it. That layer changes the meaning of none of I, N, F or P.

Introversion describes a tendency to direct attention and energy inward. Intuition gives more weight to patterns and possibilities when taking in information. Feeling gives more weight to values and effects on people when making decisions. Perceiving describes a preference for keeping options open in the external world. The [INFP base page](/en/personality/infp) explains these four preferences. The [NERIS account of Identity](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent) describes the separate Assertive and Turbulent ends.

In a fictional example, a colleague says a permissions guide still leaves new members unsure what they can change. Two writers could ask the same follow-up question. One might remain confident that the rest is clear. The other might begin to worry about their ability to write instructions. Either person can make the same correction once the gap is clear.

Both feelings are only examples. The same person can land on different sides in different settings: more assured with familiar content, more doubtful the first time they take on an unfamiliar system with a same-day deadline. Only with the duty, the experience and the deadline in view does a comparison mean anything.

body: The table lists six observation scenes, each comparing the two under the same information, deadline and duty. Only self-assessment and response to pressure are compared. Either end can carry out the same checking and revision, and the action and its timing are decided by the same evidence and duty.

| Observation (same situation, same duty) | INFP-A (Assertive) | INFP-T (Turbulent) | What this row compares |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A reader says, “New members can’t follow this notice” | May still feel confident about the rest of the notice | May feel less confident that the notice as a whole is clear | Identity: self-assessment |
| After both confirm the same problem with the QR code | May still feel confident about the other decisions that went into the notice | May start to doubt those same decisions | Identity: self-assessment |
| The feeling when a mistake is pointed out | May treat the feedback as an assessment of this one notice | May extend the same sentence into a worry about their writing ability | Identity: self-assessment |
| The deadline is close and both are dealing with the same demand at home | Under that pressure, may still feel confident about the original judgment | Under that pressure, may feel less certain about the original judgment | Identity: pressure response and self-assessment |
| After the same notice is sent to the wrong group | May see it as a specific mistake and stay confident about their other decisions | May take it as a reason to doubt whether they are suited to this kind of work | Identity: self-assessment |
| After explaining the same change to the same audience | May still feel confident about how they handled the change | May worry more about how the audience will judge their handling of the change | Identity: pressure response and self-assessment |

If the verified problem leaves only one compliant fix, either end can adopt it. Even with the same fix, one may still trust its other judgements while the other keeps doubting its own. What is compared here is self-assessment under the same conditions; whether to change anything is decided by the evidence.

You can ask next what new information would change the handling. If the figures are confirmed wrong and affect eligibility, either end can check the original material immediately; if it is only a matter of wording preference, both can wait for trial-reader feedback before deciding. Consequences and evidence decide the next step, and self-assessment may shift with the situation.

body: All three scenes below are fictional, used only to look back at self-assessment and the feeling of pressure. Whether and how something should change depends separately on reader feedback, the original agreement and the process record.
### INFP-A and INFP-T receive the same reader criticism
In this fictional example, two people write notices for a community reading group using the same template. A reader tells both writers they cannot find where to sign up.

In this fictional example, both writers find a QR code with no text telling readers what it opens. Both label the code and provide clear sign-up instructions. One may still feel confident about the rest of the notice. The other may wonder whether they are good at writing notices at all. If trial readers still cannot access the form, check the registration link or offer another way to sign up. Neither writer’s confidence answers that access question.
### INFP-A and INFP-T face the same last-minute request
(A fictional scene.) A friend wants to hand over the shopping for a weekend gathering at short notice, both have already taken on other tasks, and what was agreed before was only the use of a venue.

Either may go back over the conversation to confirm the division, then reply: "I will open up, and the shopping needs someone else." In this fictional scene, once the same division is made clear, one may still be confident about the reply while the other worries more that the refusal will be read as unkind. The original agreement and the other person's reply help confirm the boundary; the worry itself cannot prove how the other person understood it.
### INFP-A and INFP-T handle the same delivery mistake
(A fictional scene.) Suppose the attachment went out as last week's version, to the same recipients and with the same deadline.

Either may first tell the recipients to stop using it and send the correct file, then go back to the naming, the shared folder and the permissions. The difference comes after the resend: having both resent it, one may see it as one specific mistake and stay confident about the other judgements, while the other may doubt its own thoroughness more. Together you can record whether the wrong file was withdrawn, whether the recipients could open the right version, and whether the same risk would affect the next delivery; if repeated checking can no longer change those results, move it into a routine review. If the cause was two files with the same name in the shared folder, the fix is a distinctive naming convention; if it happened only after one network failure, the next step is asking the recipients to confirm the upload. Either handling is more direct than judging that the person "needs to be more confident".

body: Reading A as "mentally strong" and T as "overthinking" is the most common misreading. These two NERIS words mark the default landing point of self-assessment; they are not a score for resilience, and they do not measure ability.

The second misreading is judging the end from an action. Who rereads first, who asks about details first, can all be seen in one event, yet says nothing about the suffix — either end may check, and either may not. Someone replying "got it, I will answer tonight" may be verifying something, or may be looking after a child; guessing a suffix from the speed of a reply turns a schedule into a personality.

The third misreading is treating the suffix as filling a slot in the four letters. A/T is a separate layer in a 16Personalities NERIS report; it changes none of INFP's four letters and is not a fifth official MBTI dimension. The second letter is still N, the third still F, and the part after the hyphen does not stack onto a preference.

The fourth misreading is taking one fluctuation as a conclusion. A retest may give a different suffix, but the change itself points to no single explanation: it may be a different stretch of experience being drawn on, or a different situation at the time. Self-assessment and the assessment of others can also come apart: someone confident about their own decisions may still listen carefully to how a friend reacted to an arrangement, and someone who often questions their own work may still not guess on a friend's behalf what that friend needs.

body: This section offers a comparison of situations, not a choice of sides. The same person's reaction can land on different sides in different situations, and writing down the conditions is more useful than pinning a label on yourself.

When a piece of work is found to have one problem, you can check at the same time whether the feedback is specific and how much assurance remains about the original judgement after the revision. Both may make the same revision, and the same person's self-assessment also shifts with the situation. A review is only for understanding the experience; it cannot determine a suffix.

Use this exercise to understand how feedback affected your confidence. It gives no A/T result. Choose a recent event and record the words you heard, what you thought of your work at the time, and how you felt the next day. For example, did you see one unclear paragraph or start doubting your ability to write? Use the record to decide what to ask for next time, such as a specific example and its effect on the reader.

The record keeps only the information available at the time. If you learn later that the criticism was not accurate, write that fact into the result, so that the first reaction is not judged by what you only learned afterwards. If you hit a particularly memorable but atypical example, find an ordinary small example to compare with it. If this kind of unease persistently affects sleep, eating or work, professional support should be sought, rather than judging by comparison pages. If two attempts give different suffixes, you can compare the scale, the scores and the situation at the time, and keep whatever cannot yet be determined.

body: **Framework sources.** The definitions of the two ends follow the [NERIS account of Identity](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent): Identity is a NERIS dimension from 16Personalities, Assertive and Turbulent are its two ends, and it covers self-assessment, self-assurance and response to pressure; it is not a fifth official MBTI dimension. The four-letter preferences belong to a separate type description, and the two do not replace each other.

**Function notation.** This page uses Fi–Ne–Si–Te, a common way to write INFP’s theoretical function stack. The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists both Si and Se for tertiary Sensing. The source convention applies to both suffixes. It gives no basis for ranking ability or predicting behaviour.

**Editorial fiction statement.** The community reading group notice and the "newcomers cannot follow it" feedback, the permissions guide and the "a new member still cannot tell what they can change" feedback, the reader who cannot find the sign-up entry, the friend's last-minute request for weekend shopping, the attachment sent as last week's version, the notice sent to the wrong group, explaining a change in public, the instructor pointing out wrong figures in the material, and the details of each resend and confirmation of the division are all editorial fiction, used only for practice in telling things apart, and correspond to no real person or event.

**Scope limits.** This comparison is not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability; A/T does not measure the quality of a judgement, nor can it be used to infer which end is more common. Results have to be read together with the setting in which the questions were answered and recent experience; health and safety matters follow professional guidance, with clinical judgement resting on a qualified professional. The FermatMind assessment uses a different item bank and scoring, and this page does not assume from the NERIS account that its scoring is the same; the differences are set out in the [assessment method and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

body: The two have exactly the same four letters, and even the function order does not change with the suffix. The difference appears only in the Identity layer inside a 16Personalities report: one end is more at ease with its own judgement, the other more readily doubts it. That layer changes the meaning of none of I, N, F or P.

Introversion describes a tendency to direct attention and energy inward. Intuition gives more weight to patterns and possibilities when taking in information. Feeling gives more weight to values and effects on people when making decisions. Perceiving describes a preference for keeping options open in the external world. The [INFP base page](/en/personality/infp) explains these four preferences. The [NERIS account of Identity](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent) describes the separate Assertive and Turbulent ends.

In a fictional example, a colleague says a permissions guide still leaves new members unsure what they can change. Two writers could ask the same follow-up question. One might remain confident that the rest is clear. The other might begin to worry about their ability to write instructions. Either person can make the same correction once the gap is clear.

Both feelings are only examples. The same person can land on different sides in different settings: more assured with familiar content, more doubtful the first time they take on an unfamiliar system with a same-day deadline. Only with the duty, the experience and the deadline in view does a comparison mean anything.

You can ask next what new information would change the handling. body: All three scenes below are fictional, used only to look back at self-assessment and the feeling of pressure. Whether and how something should change depends separately on reader feedback, the original agreement and the process record.
### INFP-A and INFP-T receive the same reader criticism
In this fictional example, two people write notices for a community reading group using the same template. A reader tells both writers they cannot find where to sign up.

In this fictional example, both writers find a QR code with no text telling readers what it opens. Both label the code and provide clear sign-up instructions. One may still feel confident about the rest of the notice. The other may wonder whether they are good at writing notices at all. If trial readers still cannot access the form, check the registration link or offer another way to sign up. Neither writer’s confidence answers that access question.
### INFP-A and INFP-T face the same last-minute request
(A fictional scene.) A friend wants to hand over the shopping for a weekend gathering at short notice, both have already taken on other tasks, and what was agreed before was only the use of a venue.

Either may go back over the conversation to confirm the division, then reply: "I will open up, and the shopping needs someone else." In this fictional scene, once the same division is made clear, one may still be confident about the reply while the other worries more that the refusal will be read as unkind. The original agreement and the other person's reply help confirm the boundary; the worry itself cannot prove how the other person understood it.
### INFP-A and INFP-T handle the same delivery mistake
(A fictional scene.) Suppose the attachment went out as last week's version, to the same recipients and with the same deadline.

Either may first tell the recipients to stop using it and send the correct file, then go back to the naming, the shared folder and the permissions. The difference comes after the resend: having both resent it, one may see it as one specific mistake and stay confident about the other judgements, while the other may doubt its own thoroughness more. Together you can record whether the wrong file was withdrawn, whether the recipients could open the right version, and whether the same risk would affect the next delivery; if repeated checking can no longer change those results, move it into a routine review. If the cause was two files with the same name in the shared folder, the fix is a distinctive naming convention; if it happened only after one network failure, the next step is asking the recipients to confirm the upload. Either handling is more direct than judging that the person "needs to be more confident".

body: Reading A as "mentally strong" and T as "overthinking" is the most common misreading. These two NERIS words mark the default landing point of self-assessment; they are not a score for resilience, and they do not measure ability.

The second misreading is judging the end from an action. Who rereads first, who asks about details first, can all be seen in one event, yet says nothing about the suffix — either end may check, and either may not. Someone replying "got it, I will answer tonight" may be verifying something, or may be looking after a child; guessing a suffix from the speed of a reply turns a schedule into a personality.

The third misreading is treating the suffix as filling a slot in the four letters. A/T is a separate layer in a 16Personalities NERIS report; it changes none of INFP's four letters and is not a fifth official MBTI dimension. The second letter is still N, the third still F, and the part after the hyphen does not stack onto a preference.

The fourth misreading is taking one fluctuation as a conclusion. A retest may give a different suffix, but the change itself points to no single explanation: it may be a different stretch of experience being drawn on, or a different situation at the time. Self-assessment and the assessment of others can also come apart: someone confident about their own decisions may still listen carefully to how a friend reacted to an arrangement, and someone who often questions their own work may still not guess on a friend's behalf what that friend needs.

body: This section offers a comparison of situations, not a choice of sides. The same person's reaction can land on different sides in different situations, and writing down the conditions is more useful than pinning a label on yourself.

When a piece of work is found to have one problem, you can check at the same time whether the feedback is specific and how much assurance remains about the original judgement after the revision. Both may make the same revision, and the same person's self-assessment also shifts with the situation. A review is only for understanding the experience; it cannot determine a suffix.

Use this exercise to understand how feedback affected your confidence. It gives no A/T result. Choose a recent event and record the words you heard, what you thought of your work at the time, and how you felt the next day. For example, did you see one unclear paragraph or start doubting your ability to write? Use the record to decide what to ask for next time, such as a specific example and its effect on the reader.

The record keeps only the information available at the time. If you learn later that the criticism was not accurate, write that fact into the result, so that the first reaction is not judged by what you only learned afterwards. If you hit a particularly memorable but atypical example, find an ordinary small example to compare with it. If this kind of unease persistently affects sleep, eating or work, professional support should be sought, rather than judging by comparison pages. If two attempts give different suffixes, you can compare the scale, the scores and the situation at the time, and keep whatever cannot yet be determined.

body: **Framework sources.** The definitions of the two ends follow the [NERIS account of Identity](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent): Identity is a NERIS dimension from 16Personalities, Assertive and Turbulent are its two ends, and it covers self-assessment, self-assurance and response to pressure; it is not a fifth official MBTI dimension. The four-letter preferences belong to a separate type description, and the two do not replace each other.

**Function notation.** This page uses Fi–Ne–Si–Te, a common way to write INFP’s theoretical function stack. The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists both Si and Se for tertiary Sensing. The source convention applies to both suffixes. It gives no basis for ranking ability or predicting behaviour.

**Editorial fiction statement.** The community reading group notice and the "newcomers cannot follow it" feedback, the permissions guide and the "a new member still cannot tell what they can change" feedback, the reader who cannot find the sign-up entry, the friend's last-minute request for weekend shopping, the attachment sent as last week's version, the notice sent to the wrong group, explaining a change in public, the instructor pointing out wrong figures in the material, and the details of each resend and confirmation of the division are all editorial fiction, used only for practice in telling things apart, and correspond to no real person or event.

**Scope limits.** This comparison is not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability; A/T does not measure the quality of a judgement, nor can it be used to infer which end is more common. Results have to be read together with the setting in which the questions were answered and recent experience; health and safety matters follow professional guidance, with clinical judgement resting on a qualified professional. The FermatMind assessment uses a different item bank and scoring, and this page does not assume from the NERIS account that its scoring is the same; the differences are set out in the [assessment method and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

summary_blocks.body:
INFP-A (Assertive) and INFP-T (Turbulent) share the same INFP code. In 16Personalities’ NERIS Identity dimension, the Assertive end describes steadier confidence under pressure, while the Turbulent end describes more self-doubt and greater sensitivity to stress or feedback. Official MBTI uses four preference pairs. The suffix gives no basis for judging skill or predicting how someone will respond.

INFP stands for Introversion, Intuition, Feeling and Perceiving. In MBTI type dynamics, one common notation is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Neither suffix changes the four letters or those theoretical roles.

The F in INFP means Feeling. A T in that position would mean Thinking, as in INTP. The separate -T suffix in INFP-T means Turbulent.

Two people told that newcomers cannot follow their notice may ask the same questions and make the same revision. One may still feel confident about the rest of the draft, while the other may start questioning more of their work. How quickly either person acts or feels better gives no basis for assigning a suffix.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
The two have exactly the same four letters, and even the function order does not change with the suffix. The difference appears only in the Identity layer inside a 16Personalities report: one end is more at ease with its own judgement, the other more readily doubts it. That layer changes the meaning of none of I, N, F or P.

Introversion describes a tendency to direct attention and energy inward. Intuition gives more weight to patterns and possibilities when taking in information. Feeling gives more weight to values and effects on people when making decisions. Perceiving describes a preference for keeping options open in the external world. The [INFP base page](/en/personality/infp) explains these four preferences. The [NERIS account of Identity](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent) describes the separate Assertive and Turbulent ends.

In a fictional example, a colleague says a permissions guide still leaves new members unsure what they can change. Two writers could ask the same follow-up question. One might remain confident that the rest is clear. The other might begin to worry about their ability to write instructions. Either person can make the same correction once the gap is clear.

Both feelings are only examples. The same person can land on different sides in different settings: more assured with familiar content, more doubtful the first time they take on an unfamiliar system with a same-day deadline. Only with the duty, the experience and the deadline in view does a comparison mean anything.
sections.title: INFP-A and INFP-T: what they share and where they differ

sections.body_md:
The table lists six observation scenes, each comparing the two under the same information, deadline and duty. Only self-assessment and response to pressure are compared. Either end can carry out the same checking and revision, and the action and its timing are decided by the same evidence and duty.

| Observation (same situation, same duty) | INFP-A (Assertive) | INFP-T (Turbulent) | What this row compares |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A reader says, “New members can’t follow this notice” | May still feel confident about the rest of the notice | May feel less confident that the notice as a whole is clear | Identity: self-assessment |
| After both confirm the same problem with the QR code | May still feel confident about the other decisions that went into the notice | May start to doubt those same decisions | Identity: self-assessment |
| The feeling when a mistake is pointed out | May treat the feedback as an assessment of this one notice | May extend the same sentence into a worry about their writing ability | Identity: self-assessment |
| The deadline is close and both are dealing with the same demand at home | Under that pressure, may still feel confident about the original judgment | Under that pressure, may feel less certain about the original judgment | Identity: pressure response and self-assessment |
| After the same notice is sent to the wrong group | May see it as a specific mistake and stay confident about their other decisions | May take it as a reason to doubt whether they are suited to this kind of work | Identity: self-assessment |
| After explaining the same change to the same audience | May still feel confident about how they handled the change | May worry more about how the audience will judge their handling of the change | Identity: pressure response and self-assessment |

If the verified problem leaves only one compliant fix, either end can adopt it. Even with the same fix, one may still trust its other judgements while the other keeps doubting its own. What is compared here is self-assessment under the same conditions; whether to change anything is decided by the evidence.

You can ask next what new information would change the handling. If the figures are confirmed wrong and affect eligibility, either end can check the original material immediately; if it is only a matter of wording preference, both can wait for trial-reader feedback before deciding. Consequences and evidence decide the next step, and self-assessment may shift with the situation.
sections.title: INFP-A and INFP-T: the difference in a minute

sections.body_md:
All three scenes below are fictional, used only to look back at self-assessment and the feeling of pressure. Whether and how something should change depends separately on reader feedback, the original agreement and the process record.

### INFP-A and INFP-T receive the same reader criticism

In this fictional example, two people write notices for a community reading group using the same template. A reader tells both writers they cannot find where to sign up.

In this fictional example, both writers find a QR code with no text telling readers what it opens. Both label the code and provide clear sign-up instructions. One may still feel confident about the rest of the notice. The other may wonder whether they are good at writing notices at all. If trial readers still cannot access the form, check the registration link or offer another way to sign up. Neither writer’s confidence answers that access question.

### INFP-A and INFP-T face the same last-minute request

(A fictional scene.) A friend wants to hand over the shopping for a weekend gathering at short notice, both have already taken on other tasks, and what was agreed before was only the use of a venue.

Either may go back over the conversation to confirm the division, then reply: "I will open up, and the shopping needs someone else." In this fictional scene, once the same division is made clear, one may still be confident about the reply while the other worries more that the refusal will be read as unkind. The original agreement and the other person's reply help confirm the boundary; the worry itself cannot prove how the other person understood it.

### INFP-A and INFP-T handle the same delivery mistake

(A fictional scene.) Suppose the attachment went out as last week's version, to the same recipients and with the same deadline.

Either may first tell the recipients to stop using it and send the correct file, then go back to the naming, the shared folder and the permissions. The difference comes after the resend: having both resent it, one may see it as one specific mistake and stay confident about the other judgements, while the other may doubt its own thoroughness more. Together you can record whether the wrong file was withdrawn, whether the recipients could open the right version, and whether the same risk would affect the next delivery; if repeated checking can no longer change those results, move it into a routine review. If the cause was two files with the same name in the shared folder, the fix is a distinctive naming convention; if it happened only after one network failure, the next step is asking the recipients to confirm the upload. Either handling is more direct than judging that the person "needs to be more confident".
sections.title: INFP-A and INFP-T: work and relationship scenes

sections.body_md:
Reading A as "mentally strong" and T as "overthinking" is the most common misreading. These two NERIS words mark the default landing point of self-assessment; they are not a score for resilience, and they do not measure ability.

The second misreading is judging the end from an action. Who rereads first, who asks about details first, can all be seen in one event, yet says nothing about the suffix — either end may check, and either may not. Someone replying "got it, I will answer tonight" may be verifying something, or may be looking after a child; guessing a suffix from the speed of a reply turns a schedule into a personality.

The third misreading is treating the suffix as filling a slot in the four letters. A/T is a separate layer in a 16Personalities NERIS report; it changes none of INFP's four letters and is not a fifth official MBTI dimension. The second letter is still N, the third still F, and the part after the hyphen does not stack onto a preference.

The fourth misreading is taking one fluctuation as a conclusion. A retest may give a different suffix, but the change itself points to no single explanation: it may be a different stretch of experience being drawn on, or a different situation at the time. Self-assessment and the assessment of others can also come apart: someone confident about their own decisions may still listen carefully to how a friend reacted to an arrangement, and someone who often questions their own work may still not guess on a friend's behalf what that friend needs.
sections.title: INFP-A and INFP-T: common misreadings

sections.body_md:
This section offers a comparison of situations, not a choice of sides. The same person's reaction can land on different sides in different situations, and writing down the conditions is more useful than pinning a label on yourself.

When a piece of work is found to have one problem, you can check at the same time whether the feedback is specific and how much assurance remains about the original judgement after the revision. Both may make the same revision, and the same person's self-assessment also shifts with the situation. A review is only for understanding the experience; it cannot determine a suffix.

Use this exercise to understand how feedback affected your confidence. It gives no A/T result. Choose a recent event and record the words you heard, what you thought of your work at the time, and how you felt the next day. For example, did you see one unclear paragraph or start doubting your ability to write? Use the record to decide what to ask for next time, such as a specific example and its effect on the reader.

The record keeps only the information available at the time. If you learn later that the criticism was not accurate, write that fact into the result, so that the first reaction is not judged by what you only learned afterwards. If you hit a particularly memorable but atypical example, find an ordinary small example to compare with it. If this kind of unease persistently affects sleep, eating or work, professional support should be sought, rather than judging by comparison pages. If two attempts give different suffixes, you can compare the scale, the scores and the situation at the time, and keep whatever cannot yet be determined.
sections.title: INFP-A and INFP-T: how to keep observing yourself

items.answer:
The difference is on the Identity dimension of NERIS: the A end trusts its own judgement more and is less disturbed by pressure, while the T end doubts itself more readily and is more sensitive to pressure. These are two ends of one dimension, not two kinds of INFP.

After the same comment about an unclear notice, two people can ask for an example, reread their drafts and make the same change. What may differ is how much confidence each retains in their original judgment. An isolated response cannot establish a suffix.
items.question: What is the main difference between INFP-A and INFP-T?

items.answer:
Neither is decided by the suffix. Handling criticism well depends on understanding the problem, checking the facts and completing a revision that is useful to readers.

One person may still trust most of their original judgment after a correction. Another may question more of their work. Either can understand the criticism and make a useful revision. Check any factual issue first, clarify the goal if the comment is about style, and see whether readers can actually complete the task.
items.question: Which of INFP-A and INFP-T handles criticism better?

items.answer:
Not because of the A/T suffix. In MBTI type dynamics the function order is explained by the four-letter type and the theoretical writing adopted; A/T is an Identity marking in the 16Personalities NERIS report, not a fifth official MBTI dimension.

The four-letter code looks the same in both sets of material, and the meaning still has to be read against each. To check the function order, look at the base type and the writing that source uses; to check the suffix, look at how the report defines self-assessment and response to pressure. Keep the two questions apart and the suffix will not be used to infer the strength of a function.
items.question: Does the function order differ between INFP-A and INFP-T?

items.answer:
Check the version of the assessment, the experience you drew on when answering, and whether the dimension scores sit close to the dividing line; these three are worth more attention than "which time was more accurate".

One time you might have answered with familiar work in mind, and another time with recent public criticism in mind. Compare the assessment, score context and situations before interpreting a change. One result change cannot show whether the difference arose from measurement, circumstances or a lasting change.
items.question: Why does the result sometimes come out INFP-A and sometimes INFP-T?

items.answer:
There is no need to choose a job by suffix. The suffix concerns self-assessment and response to pressure, while a career judgement depends on the actual tasks, the working environment and the results of trying something yourself.

Try a task that includes getting feedback and making a revision. Ask who usually gives feedback, what counts as complete and how many stages the work goes through. If you enjoy the task but find the feedback process draining, compare how another team works. Use the [FermatMind career library](/en/career) to find a role’s core duties and pick one small task to try.
items.question: Do INFP-A and INFP-T need different jobs?

items.answer:
It depends what you are missing: the base of the four letters, or the detail of one end.

The full account of the four preferences is on the [INFP base page](/en/personality/infp); for one end only, read [INFP-A](/en/personality/infp-a) or [INFP-T](/en/personality/infp-t). It helps to write down the question you have now, then choose the entry point, and to bring one real example that can be checked.

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources.** The definitions of the two ends follow the [NERIS account of Identity](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent): Identity is a NERIS dimension from 16Personalities, Assertive and Turbulent are its two ends, and it covers self-assessment, self-assurance and response to pressure; it is not a fifth official MBTI dimension. The four-letter preferences belong to a separate type description, and the two do not replace each other.

**Function notation.** This page uses Fi–Ne–Si–Te, a common way to write INFP’s theoretical function stack. The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists both Si and Se for tertiary Sensing. The source convention applies to both suffixes. It gives no basis for ranking ability or predicting behaviour.

**Editorial fiction statement.** The community reading group notice and the "newcomers cannot follow it" feedback, the permissions guide and the "a new member still cannot tell what they can change" feedback, the reader who cannot find the sign-up entry, the friend's last-minute request for weekend shopping, the attachment sent as last week's version, the notice sent to the wrong group, explaining a change in public, the instructor pointing out wrong figures in the material, and the details of each resend and confirmation of the division are all editorial fiction, used only for practice in telling things apart, and correspond to no real person or event.

**Scope limits.** This comparison is not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability; A/T does not measure the quality of a judgement, nor can it be used to infer which end is more common. Results have to be read together with the setting in which the questions were answered and recent experience; health and safety matters follow professional guidance, with clinical judgement resting on a qualified professional. The FermatMind assessment uses a different item bank and scoring, and this page does not assume from the NERIS account that its scoring is the same; the differences are set out in the [assessment method and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

The FermatMind editorial team
